messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar Haddad, a 37-year-old married firefighter, described the beginning of the problem as something that at first seemed too strange and minor to call dangerous. Months earlier, after a community fire safety event, he began noticing the same man appearing near the station, outside the grocery store his wife used, and along the route he sometimes took home. The man was often on a bicycle. At first Omar told himself there had to be a harmless explanation, but the sightings accumulated in specific places until those places themselves began to feel contaminated. He would pull into the station parking lot and feel his chest tighten before he had even gotten out of the truck, already looking for that bike. On one occasion he left a hardware store and saw the cyclist across the street, stopped and watching him. Another time, while driving home, he caught sight of the bicycle pacing traffic along the side street and became convinced he was being tracked deliberately, his movements known in advance. What frightened him most was not a single confrontation but the repeated experience that he could be found anywhere.

In the weeks that followed, Omar moved through the city as if the threat were still active in every block and doorway. Physical locations where he had seen the man took on a charge of their own. Passing the store parking lot or the side street where the bicycle had appeared could bring the whole experience back in an instant, without warning, as though the present had dropped away. He said that when that happened he was overcome so quickly that he had to stop what he was doing; if he tried to talk about what had happened in those moments, he often lost his words. He knew the sequence of events perfectly well, but in session he would stall out, look down, and say he could not explain it properly. The emotional force of the memory seemed to arrive all at once, more as a full-body state than a story he could calmly tell.

At work the pattern became especially visible. Omar had spent years entering burning buildings where alertness was part of the job, and he now found himself unable to set that vigilance down in ordinary settings. If he walked into a restaurant with his crew after a shift, he scanned for exits immediately and kept track of who was near the doors. At department briefings he noticed every unexpected clang, radio burst, or slammed locker, his body jerking to attention before he could think. He watched other people closely, searching their faces and movements for signs of danger, and if someone lingered too long outside the station or slowed near the apparatus bay, his focus narrowed onto them. He did not describe this as irrational. From his point of view, it was what made sense after learning that someone could appear repeatedly and silently in the background of his life.

Outside work, the sense of being followed had spread into daily routines with his wife. A cyclist approaching from behind on the street could make him turn around repeatedly to check whether the person stayed with him through several blocks. In parking lots and building lobbies he positioned himself where he could see entrances and exits. He began avoiding certain locations entirely, especially places where he had previously seen the stalker or where bicycles were common. Over time this shrank the couple’s routines. Errands were rerouted, restaurants dropped, and simple outings became negotiations about where Omar would feel able to go. His wife noticed that he rarely relaxed once they were out; he was always monitoring, listening, looking over shoulders, studying whether anyone seemed too interested in them.

What troubled Omar nearly as much as the fear was what he had come to believe about himself. He was a firefighter, someone others relied on in emergencies, and he could not reconcile that identity with how shaken he felt by stalking. He had begun to think he had permanently changed for the worse. He said he was not the same man who could once move through the world without calculating escape routes. At his lowest moments he wondered if his reactions meant he was going crazy, especially when a sound or a familiar location brought back the entire experience so suddenly that he felt seized by it. He also judged himself harshly for struggling at all, privately concluding that a stronger person would have handled it better and that his continued fear proved some weakness in him.

By the time he sought help, Omar was exhausted by the constant readiness and ashamed of how much space the stalking had taken up in his marriage and daily life. What finally pushed him into treatment was not one dramatic incident but the accumulation of them: another abrupt surge of fear when he noticed a bicycle near a familiar intersection, another meal spent with his back to the wall counting exits, another attempt to explain himself to his wife that dissolved into silence because he could not find the words. He came in wanting relief, but also wanting to know whether he could trust his own mind again. What he feared most was that this watchfulness and sense of damage were now permanent; what he hoped was that he might still be able to live in his city, do his job, and walk into a room without feeling hunted.
